text: Learning which items belong to which person.

Wake someone up; help someone sit, stand, or steady themselves; offer an arm on stairs; help with buttons, zips, and shoes; fetch and clean glasses and hearing aids; push or fold a wheelchair or walker.
Maintain other household robots: empty the robot vacuum, clean its brushes, refill the mop tank, rescue it when stuck, clear cords and socks before it runs.

Situational variations. Apartments and condos (elevators, shared laundry, HOA rules), regional standards (metric vs. imperial, front vs. top-load, induction vs. gas, shoes-off homes), languages, accents, and speech differences, residents with disabilities or dementia, residents' emotional states, and robot-side degradation (dirty camera, low battery, network down, a failing arm).
“Make this place look nice.” There may be no single correct state; it has to reason about symmetry, spacing, aesthetics, furniture placement, and household preferences.
“Fix this up.” The robot must determine what looks wrong before deciding what actions to take.
“Make the house presentable before guests arrive.” It must prioritize visible problems rather than blindly deep-cleaning everything.
“You have ten minutes. Make this look better.” The robot must optimize its action sequence.
“Finish whatever I forgot to do.” It needs to inspect the environment and infer incomplete chores.
“Get the house ready for the morning.” It might prepare coffee equipment, bags, clothes, lunch items, blinds, and room temperature.
“Prepare everything I’ll need tomorrow.” Requires reasoning from calendar/context, weather, activities, school/work needs, and personal habits.
“Pack for a weekend trip.” Requires selecting clothing and supplies based on duration, weather, planned activities, and available luggage space.
“Pack the fragile stuff carefully.” It has to recognize fragility and invent appropriate packing strategies.
“Make this fit in the box.” Requires spatial reasoning, rotation, rearrangement, folding, and possibly choosing another box.
“Find something soft to protect this.” It must select padding from unrelated household items.
“Find where the dog took my sock.” Requires reasoning about pet behavior.
“Make my room how it was yesterday.” Requires state reconstruction.
“Untie this knot.” Requires understanding knot topology.
“Zip this bag even though it’s really full.” Requires rearranging contents and controlling deformation.
“Get everything outside that shouldn’t get wet.” Requires material and ownership reasoning.
“Do it without moving the sleeping baby.” Requires low-noise, low-vibration planning.
“Sort this pile into what we keep, donate, and throw away.” Requires household preferences and sometimes asking for confirmation.

“We’re out of paper towels; find something else to clean this up.” The robot must evaluate the nature of the spill (oil, water, biohazard) and find a suitable, safe alternative (a rag, a sponge, newspaper) without ruining a nice towel.
“Is it dry yet?” (laundry, paint, a mopped floor) Requires judging state from sparse cues.
“Can this go in the microwave / dishwasher / dryer?” Requires reasoning about materials, labels, and safety.
“Keep the meat and dairy dishes separate.” / “Shoes stay off.” / “Don’t touch Grandpa’s chair.” Requires picking up household rules, including cultural or sentimental ones that look arbitrary.
